articles.title: Is India investing enough in disaster risk reduction? - Down To Earth
articles.full_text:
India has significantly improved its disaster response, with Odisha evacuating 1.2 million people ahead of Cyclone Fani in 2019, two decades after a super cyclone killed nearly 10,000 people.
The Sixteenth Finance Commission has earmarked Rs 2.84 lakh crore for disaster management between 2026 and 2031, but funding remains heavily skewed towards relief rather than prevention.
Disasters cost India an estimated 0.4% of GDP annually, according to the OECD, highlighting the economic consequences of extreme weather events.
Early warning systems must translate forecasts into timely action, while infrastructure needs to be designed for a changing climate.
Investing in locally tailored disaster plans, community preparedness and natural ecosystems can help protect homes, livelihoods and infrastructure.
The International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction served as a reminder to reassess disaster preparedness and ensure that it keeps pace with climate change and the growing intensity of extreme weather events.
In 1999, a super cyclone killed nearly 10,000 people in Odisha. Two decades later, cyclone Fani, the strongest storm to hit the state since, prompted the evacuation of a record 1.2 million people in less than 48 hours. The official death toll was 64. Every death was a tragedy, but the loss of life was far lower than it might have been. Few countries have improved so much, so quickly, at moving people out of harm’s way.
Fani also damaged more than 350,000 homes, brought down power lines and flattened coastal trees. Families survived, but much of what they had built did not. That is the next frontier: having learned to save lives, we must now learn to protect livelihoods and the homes, roads, crops, water systems and forests that communities depend on long after the storm has passed.
The need to do more is growing more urgent. Floods, cyclones, heatwaves and wildfires are becoming more frequent and intense. This year, floods killed about 100 people in Assam, landslides struck Kerala, cloudbursts killed about 31 in Jammu and Kashmir, and lightning claimed 14 lives in Jharkhand, most of them farm workers. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) estimates that disasters cost India about 0.4 per cent of GDP a year.
